Citing various texts throughout his work to encompass the teachings of an entire lifetime,
the formal style and primary intent of his writings converge solely upon two sutras:
first, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, by means of which he clarifies the reality of the "original" and "traced" aspects.
Second, relying on *nirvāṇa* to support the *vinaya* and reveal the permanence [of the Buddha-nature],
because these two sūtras are identical to the *amṛta* (the finest essence). Therefore,
the *Śeṣanāmanirukti-śāstra* discusses their relative dependence and their ultimate transcendence.
This extends even to the partial and the perfect.

the four "ones" of Guangzhai are fully utilized to clarify their function.
This means that true reality (*tathatā*) is the essential substance of practice.

the concluding section of the "Arising" chapter offers a general eulogy, stating:
Having diligently sought it through accumulated kalpas, he has realized it at the site of enlightenment.
Śāriputra’s three requests and the Buddha’s three explanations of the Dharma through parables—

Thus we know that these four kinds of samādhi all rely upon the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa).

the four conditions are the practice of peace and bliss.

The purpose of initiating the teaching is solely to enable sentient beings to open, show, awaken to, and enter [the Dharma].
The ultimate aim is simply to return to the wondrous Dharma’s secret treasury of the three tracks.
Thus, from beginning to end, everything relies upon the Lotus Sūtra;
this is precisely the sublime practice of the Lotus Samādhi.
Next, regarding the use of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*:
although all [teachings] rely on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and ultimately return to the single reality (*eka-tattva*),
if there is no assistance for those of dull faculties in the final age, [they will not attain liberation].
Then, correct practice will collapse;
only when correct practice and its aids mutually reinforce one another can they proceed far.
Even the Buddha’s transformation [of beings] takes nirvana as its life-span.
Moreover, in the final age, those who practice cannot advance without assistance;
therefore, the Vinaya is upheld and the permanence [of the Buddha] is taught to reveal the true mark (dharmatā).
Thus, the merit is attributed to that [Vinaya].
Therefore, by correctly employing the intent of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the perfect and eternal [nature] is revealed;
thus, the two sutras are equal.
Third, as for the method of explaining the text and its meaning:
Furthermore, there are two aspects:
first, the detailed investigation of the words and their meanings;
second, the elucidation of the underlying structure and force.
The initial section consists of two parts:
first, a detailed investigation of the textual meaning;
second, a detailed investigation of the textual characteristics.
The first consists of ten examples.
The first is citing evidence regarding the universal and the specific;
for instance, citing from the *Lotus Sūtra* a passage concerning the single reality.
Prefacing this with an account of past teachings as that which was opened [for exposition],
the texts within these sections contain both provisional and ultimate meanings;
if one intends to verify a specific ultimate truth, one cites the textual passages pertaining to that ultimate truth.
If one intends to provide a general proof for the skillful means (*upāya*), then one must also cite the former interpretations.
This is like citing the *Lotus Sūtra* to prove both the gradual and the indeterminate [teachings];
the same applies to the scope and limitations of the texts cited regarding the four flavors (*catasraḥ rasāḥ*).
Second is the "analogy of drawing forth similar categories," which refers to citing scriptural evidence to corroborate contemplation and so forth;
it is like the citation from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* stating that light first illuminates high mountains.
The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa* begins with [the Bodhisattva] sitting beneath the Bodhi tree;

the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* cites the analogy of milk being produced from cow's milk; and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* speaks of "expedient means" (*upāya-kauśalya*) and so forth—these serve as scriptural evidence for the meaning of the three types of *śamatha-vipaśyanā*.
Thus we know that while the names "gradual" and so forth used for teaching and contemplation are identical, their meanings are eternally different.
Although that text classifies the teachings, I now employ its categories by analogy;
therefore, I borrow these three names to expound my own meaning.
This means that provisional names are employed to express ultimate meanings.
For example, by citing the terminology of "repudiating and seizing" from the Vaipulya sutras,
one expresses the present meaning of "opening the provisional" and "transcending all dependencies."
The other three periods may be understood by analogy with this.
What was there termed "combined," "exclusive," "confrontational," and so forth,
now becomes "opening," "abolishing," "harmonizing," and so on.
Fourth is the "transfer by means of a metaphor," such as [the examples of] a pig rubbing against a mountain of gold and so forth.

While the treatise used these metaphors for patience (*kṣānti*) and other virtues, here they are borrowed as metaphors for tranquility (*śamatha*) and other qualities. These metaphors are worldly categories that are transferred and applied according to their underlying meaning.
Why restrict ourselves to the main text alone?
For instance, regarding the single entity of fire,
various sūtras sometimes use it as a metaphor for anger and sometimes as a metaphor for wisdom.
Alternatively, whether using illumination or burning, form or nature, essence or function,
and even when employing earth, water, wind, and so forth as metaphors, it is likewise so. Therefore,
one should not restrict the meaning to the literal text as definitive.
Fifth, citing collateral sources to distinguish [the views], as in various texts,
employing the *Abhidharmakośa* and the *Tattvasiddhi*,
whether to establish the initial stage of gradualism or to address the partial and limited [teachings].
Thus, name and meaning are borrowed together;
for example, in the two practices of faith and dharma,
at the beginning of the text, the five aggregates and the number of kings occur simultaneously.
"Other times," and so forth,
serve merely to distinguish differences rather than to borrow names and meanings.
Sixth is "opening up the general to produce the particular."
As for the texts concerning the four *siddhāntas*, the five flavors, the three provisional designations (*prajñapti*), and the two emptinesses,
their meanings encompass both opening and closing, and their significance pervades all categories;
there is no teaching that does not conform to this principle.
Seventh is the citation of essential tenets,
such as the provisional and the real, the original and the manifested in the *Lotus Sūtra*,
or the shared and unshared aspects in the *Prajñāpāramitā* teachings.
Regarding the Vaipulya, the refutations, the supernatural powers, the unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*),
and so forth— by citing even one or two phrases, one grasps the essential core of those texts;
whether refuting or establishing, one does not lose the original resonance of the school.
Eighth, regarding the citation of Confucianism and Daoism:
whether refuting or establishing [their views], one does not contravene one's own fundamental school.
This brief differentiation of similarities and differences is not intended to be exhaustive.
One does not assume that because names are similar, their meanings must be identical.
For this reason, the citations provided here are merely brief and abbreviated.
Ninth is "borrowing names while abbreviating meanings."
As in the *Saṃgrahaṇī* and in the case of the "medicines for consciousness" and so forth,
I have merely borrowed these names to illustrate their characteristics;
were I to provide a more detailed explanation, it would become excessively prolix.
Briefly pointing to the upper and lower [sections], the application of these principles can be understood by analogy.
Tenth is the application of the principle through analogy, as in the case of the two paths:
the path of instruction and the path of realization.
Originally belonging to the Separate Teaching (biejiao), it is now applied universally;
thus, two meanings are distinguished based on realization and based on exposition.

A detailed investigation of the characteristics of these texts also yields ten categories.
The first is the opening and closing according to specific characteristics,
such as the three contemplations, the four teachings, the four *siddhāntas*, the five flavors, the truths, conditions, and the *pāramitās*.
The textual expressions of the established tenets of this school are all thus:
vast and infinite, corresponding to phenomena and principles,
to dharmas and names, and to practices and realizations.
It may be employed by oneself or others without exception;
however, one must summarize it so as not to allow for superficiality or excess.
If this is not done, [the teaching will become diluted].
The articles sought do not rely on external support, and the conduct established cannot be applied elsewhere.
If one grasps the intended meaning of the present [text],
then by preserving the original phrasing, there will be a standard for both the shallow and the profound.
When expounding upon the principles of meaning, they are boundless in both length and breadth;
when demonstrating the single mind, they roll back the provisional to return to the real.
When responding to sentient beings, they open up the real to bring forth the provisional.
Establishing the rules of conduct takes wisdom as the means of penetration;
for those who dissolve all marks, not even a hair’s breadth is left behind.
Yet when preserving the various teachings, cause and effect remain clearly distinct.
To manifest this single principle, there is no duality from beginning to end.
Second, this concludes by indicating the location and explaining the intended meaning of the established text;
as in other cases, the remaining aggregates (*skandha*) and bases (*āyatana*) are treated at the end of the section on "Refuting Pervasiveness."
The "Upright Refutation of the Pervasiveness of Dharmas" contains six sections that demonstrate the sublime.
Within the section on the sublime object, it clarifies the general principles of the teaching;
in the section on the arousal of the mind, it uses the perfect to refute the partial.
Within the "Peaceful Mind," the ultimate meaning opens into three aspects;
within the "Dharma-Elements," nothing is excluded from the foundations of mindfulness;
and within the "Penetration and Obstruction," one fundamentally treats the grasping subject.
Within the subsequent stages, one is exhorted to practice the five repentances;
while patience and non-attachment are matters of advancing one's merit,
if one can trace back to the source of the fundamental principle, then all the texts will become intelligible.
Once the general outline is established, it is easy to maintain the details.
Regarding these three aspects—phenomena, principle, and their mutual correspondence—the four samādhis primarily manifest the principle while secondarily addressing heavy afflictions.
For example, the ten dharma realms primarily demonstrate the inherent nature of reality while secondarily revealing the varying degrees of depth.
In the case of the *Vijñānakāya*, the primary aim is to distinguish [the positions] from confusion, while its secondary aim is to harmonize with the sūtras.
Furthermore, in all such treatises, the refutation of ancient views serves as the secondary aim;
yet, although this intent is secondary, the primary text itself must not be discarded.
Fourth is "the phrasing being partial while the meaning is complete. This refers, for example,
to the use of the three types of cessation-and-contemplation (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*) to conclude various passages,

as well as the application of the three teachings, various objects of contemplation, and the ten stages of practice (*daśayāna*)— whether arranged vertically or horizontally, or pertaining to the partial or small vehicles— within the Fivefold Summary.
The three types of śamatha and vipaśyanā all take suchness (tathatā) as their object.
Fifth is the distinction between the extensive and the concise, and between presence and absence;
for example, as revealed in the *Bodhicittotpāda*, the enumeration is extensive while the textual description is concise.
In the section on the ten dharmas that follow, the textual exposition is extensive while the enumeration is brief;
in the section on the practice of the great path, the ritual procedures are extensive while the ten dharmas are brief;
and in the section on the cultivation of correct contemplation, the ten dharmas are extensive while the ritual procedures are brief.
The general purport of the latter three major chapters is present therein,
but it is not found in the detailed explanation.
The ten kinds of objective spheres are present within the section on correct contemplation.
The four samādhis are not present;
although they are mutually abbreviated, their meanings must necessarily be fully possessed.
Sixth, the texts and practices differ.
Just as with the sequential order of the arising of the ten objects and the ten vehicles,
and the vertical penetration of the shallow and deep levels of the ten meditations,
although the text follows a sequence, practice must necessarily accord with the individual.
Why must the ten dhyānas necessarily proceed from the shallow to the deep?
Vertically breaking through them is fundamentally for the purpose of manifesting non-duality;
alternatively, one may follow the vertical progression.
Next, as for what obstacles hinder the principle:
from the shallow to the profound, this wondrous contemplation resides therein.
Seventh is the distinction between the relative and the absolute regarding priority and sequence.
If one considers the characteristics of the teachings, the "provisional" (dai) must necessarily precede the "absolute" (zetsu).
However, if one discusses the underlying principle, the provisional and the absolute are simultaneous.
Eighth is the distinction between refuting and reconciling.
If one follows the sequence of the transformative teaching (huayi), one must first refute and subsequently harmonize;
just as one first disparages the Hinayana before later harmonizing it with the Perfect [Teaching],
the Vaipulya and Prajñāpāramitā sutras extensively refute the partial and the Hinayana.
Next, one arrives at the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* Sūtra, where one finally enters the reality.
In terms of persons and practices, the provisional and the real are simultaneously shattered and unified;
it is like illuminating the provisional in order to realize the real.
By illuminating provisional names, one breaks through and realizes true names.
Therefore, the present text aims to manifest the principle and does not,
like the *Xuanyiwen*, focus exclusively on the classification of teachings (*panjiao*).
In all instances where meanings are explained, the refutation must necessarily come first;
therefore, while the sequence of the names used here for the "partial" and "perfect" teachings borrows from that [previous] explanation, they differ in their order.
Ninth is the difference between practice and understanding.
As in the fivefold summary of the arising of conceptualization,
there are ten chapters consisting of citations of evidence, refutations of ancient views,
and the analysis of questions and answers.
This is primarily for the purpose of generating understanding. If the ten dharmas— both collectively and individually— and the ten objects mutually give rise to one another,
and the ten meditative absorptions (dhyānas)— whether separate or combined— are the manifestations of the ten objects arising specifically within practice.
Therefore, one must first gain understanding before one can engage in cultivation.
Tenth, examples are cited here by way of abbreviation;
for instance, the dharmas subsumed within the *mārga* (path) factors are [ultimately] empty and devoid of self-nature.
The remaining aggregates are refuted by analogy;
the remaining latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) and categories are illustrated by the first category;
and the continuity and mutual dependence are illustrated by the establishment of causes.
One should then minutely investigate the broad intent in order to explain the remaining texts;
by first contemplating the sequence of the dharmas, one will not obscure their essential meaning.
This applies if one is practicing the contemplation of the ten dharmas.
However, regarding the aggregates (*skandha*) and bases (*āyatana*), one must thoroughly understand their underlying causes;
as for the other nine, contemplation can only be established once they have been activated.
Therefore, among the nine objects, one distinguishes only the object of conceptualization (*vikalpa-viṣaya*).
The ten contemplations regarding the objects below are not analyzed in minute detail;
they merely follow the shifting manifestations of the objects and do not concern an extensive exposition.
Next, the explanation of their essential nature and momentum is further divided into two parts.
First, the structural form of the text;
second, the structural form of the meaning.
Regarding the first, the structural form of the text, there are also ten categories.
First, regarding the expansion and contraction of the Dharma and the analogy:
if the Dharma is concise while the analogy is extensive, one should expand the Dharma text so that it corresponds with the analogy,
rather than rigidly adhering to the concise Dharma and thereby obstructing the full expression of the analogy.
In some cases, when the Dharma is extensive and the analogy is brief, one condenses the Dharma to correspond with the analogy; in other cases, one expands the analogy to correspond with the Dharma,
such as the analogy of the wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*) for the inconceivable realm (*acintyaviṣaya*), and so forth.
Alternatively, there may be individual metaphors for the specific and a collective metaphor for the whole; for example, using a great chariot as a metaphor for ten dharmas,
whereby that collective metaphor is divided to correspond to each of the ten dharmas.
If one uses the metaphor of a hall adorned with excellent paintings,
there is no need for a detailed correspondence;
it is sufficient merely to provide a brief alignment.
If both the phenomenon (*dharma*) and the metaphor (*dṛṣṭānta*) are general,
it is like using space as a metaphor for the *dharmadhātu*.
If both the phenomenon and the metaphor are specific, they are to be correlated according to the respective textual passages.
This can be understood through the intended meaning.
Second, regarding the combination of the Dharma and its metaphors, these three may mutually exist or mutually be absent;
they are established according to what is appropriate, their presence or absence being adapted to the occasion.
Third is the opening and closing of self and other.
Generally, when enumerating chapter headings, there is an opening and closing in relation to the self,
such as the five summaries in contrast to the ten detailed expositions.
There is opening and closing in relation to others,
such as correlating the ten broad categories with the five layers of profound meaning.
There is opening and closing in terms of mutual inclusion.
As with "opening above and closing below," there is an interpretation that establishes "opening and closing," such as in the case of the *Saṃgrahaṇī* (Compendium).
The opening of the six or the four, and so forth, does not go beyond the causes and effects of self and others, as well as the four aspects of the text and the two meanings;
it resides solely within the characteristics of a single passage.
Whether expanded or contracted, its length or brevity is appropriate to the occasion.
Regarding the subsequent numbers, they must necessarily reach ten in accordance with the meaning;
thus, whether the sequence is extended or abbreviated follows what is appropriate. Fourth, regarding the "notes" (zhù) marked as "clouds" (yúnyún): [these indicate that there is more to be said].
If the preceding text already suffices,
or if other sections exist in extenso such that expanding upon them would result in prolixity,
or if the extensive text is not essential; [then one should omit it].

Fifth, regarding refutation and establishment, preservation and disappearance: those who provide commentaries must provide detailed explanations of the specific locations while summarizing and indicating the essential points;
those who transcribe the text must fill in any omissions.
Fifth, [the section on] refutation and establishment, preservation and disappearance.
Just as when refuting ancient masters or heterodox views,
once their doctrines have been demolished, there is no need to preserve them;
even if their names are retained, their meanings are not to be adopted.
If there is even the slightest point that is not appropriate, there will be rejection and acceptance;
if one refutes the biased, refutes the limited, and refutes oneself,
one must necessarily establish [one's own position] in order to perfect the inconceivable principle of one’s own school.

If one were to inquire into, respond to, examine, and investigate the characteristics of the Great and Small [vehicles]..."
Regarding the correspondence between the Dharma and its analogies, and the opening and closing of the topical gates,
one may explain them according to the text itself without needing to seek them elsewhere,
as is the case with the "Inconceivable Realm" and the "Pervasive Destruction of Dharmas."
One must observe from beginning to end to seek the middle;
one may condense the long into the short,
or expand the short into the long.
Therefore, one must first expand upon the force of the phrasing before proceeding to analyze it in detail.
Once the analysis reveals the clarity of the text, one must then integrate these fragments so that they become whole,
ensuring that the logic and phrasing flow smoothly.
This ensures that the family’s practice has a clear point of orientation.
Alternatively, there are two explanations: the general and the specific;
herein, the general serves as the heading for the specific.
In the detailed explanation of meanings, if the specific is extensive, one gathers the particulars back into the general.
Seventh is the concealment or manifestation of the dharma and the metaphor:
if the dharma is concealed and the metaphor is manifest, one seeks the meaning of the metaphor to dissolve the dharma.
If a dharma is illustrated by a metaphor, then when that illustration is obscure, one seeks the meaning of the dharma to clarify the metaphor.
The relationship between the metaphor and its application (the *upanaya*) follows this same principle of clarity and obscurity;
thus, the intent of the text is not lost, as the preceding and succeeding sections support one another.
Eighth is the inquiry and response regarding delusion and understanding.
If one is deluded in the question but not deluded in the answer,
then one formulates the question with the intent of seeking an answer.
If one is confused by the answer but not by the question,
then one investigates the wording of the question to formulate the answer;
or, the question arises from the answer.
Either one may independently resolve an obstacle,
or one may combine [the resolution] by means of an answer,
or one may formulate a challenge based on the answer.
Some answers accord with the question;
some answers contradict the question;
some answers evade the question.
Or, one may answer by opening up the inquiry.
Ninth is "citing examples to resolve the text," as in the passage on the six perfections.
Alternatively, when the force of the phrasing encompasses both, one should determine it according to the teaching so that the six modes of expression are of a single category;
whether they are truths or conditions, all phenomena are thus.
Tenth, regarding the establishment of the doctrine through the definitive teaching:
in all cases, the fundamental tenets are established in accordance with the substance of that teaching.
Sometimes the name is partial while the meaning is comprehensive, as they are determined according to the substance.
Second, the substance and force of the meaning also comprise ten categories.
First, regarding the fundamental intent of the textual divisions: whenever one wishes to explain a meaning, one should first contemplate its classification.
As in the *Fahua xuanyi*,
although "contemplating the mind" (*guanxin*) is established under each of the various meanings,
the fundamental intent of the text is to clarify that the fivefold profound meaning (*wuzhong xuanyi*) surpasses all other teachings.

Thus, the teaching of "correct contemplation" (zhèngguān) is supplemented by "contemplation based on phenomena" (tuòshì xīngguān); the principle of "establishing contemplation through the mind" (lìguān xīn) is established within the teaching,
which takes the provisional and the real, as well as the fundamental and the manifested, as its primary focus.
One constantly uses the five flavors and eight teachings to distinguish the provisional,
and employs world-systems as numerous as motes of dust to distinguish the traces.
If the fundamental and the manifested were intermingled and the flavor of the teaching were neglected,
there would be no means to reveal the two subtleties of the provisional and the ultimate;
other flavors and other sections may be sought by analogy with this principle.
Thus it can be understood.
Even if one now employs various teachings for the sake of cessation and contemplation,
the intent lies in these ten dharmas.
Having perfected the sublime contemplation, one then contemplates the primary teaching and its ancillaries;
this is to manifest the true principle.
Furthermore, by extending the understanding to all ancillary teachings, one generates faith.
First, citing various sutras from the side;
second, examining the similarities and differences among the teachings.
Since the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is taken as the standard, there must be eight types of teaching.
Although there are eight teachings,
the four teachings— Sudden and so forth— are the Buddha’s pedagogical methods;
the four teachings— Tripitaka and so forth— are the Buddha’s transformative doctrines.
When one gives rise to contemplation according to the Dharma, there are four types of contemplation.
Since these differ in their gradual progression,
they are further augmented by the indeterminate.
Therefore, there are six types of contemplation:
opening the provisional to reveal the real, and the convergence of the Tripitaka and the other two [vehicles], as well as the gradual and the indeterminate;
for one fundamentally knows that the Perfect is ultimate.
The Buddha’s original intent was solely the Buddha Vehicle (Buddhayāna).
Although, as in the present text, he follows the teachings by presenting them as either eight or four vehicles,
his fundamental purpose is solely to bring about the realization of the single Buddha Vehicle.
Third, regarding the rules for the gate of contemplation:
although the teachings are established through four gates, the essence and measure of the Dharma take non-arising as primary.
If one analyzes the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) to establish practice and understanding, [the following applies].
By refuting and selecting, and by determining the superior and the inferior, they mutually reflect one another;
all are synthesized and condensed, returning to the One Vehicle.
Fourth, it reconciles differences and examines similarities.
If all diverse names are subsumed within a single reality,
this is called "universal convergence" (*tonghui*).
It is like the convergence where all diverse names such as "following entry" (*suiru*) and "cessation" (*zhi*) and "contemplation" (*guan*) are unified.
These are called the separate assemblies.
When both the general and the separate assemblies encompass all phenomena exhaustively,
then the doctrinal power of this school’s teachings is infinite in its inclusion of all dharmas.
Even the Dharma-gates possess the significance of both general and specific assemblies.
For example, breaking through partiality to enter [the truth] is called a general assembly;
that which pertains to the specific teaching and specific gate is called a specific assembly.
Regarding the examination of similarities: as seen in the various Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna sūtras and śāstras,
although the titles and volumes of the established works differ,
their names and characteristics are not distinct.
How could one allow the Dharma to be treated as a single uniform category simply because the names are identical?
One must certainly employ reasoning to discern and distinguish them,
as is done with the various non-Buddhist outsiders.
Furthermore, since the name "Three Bodies" was established by Maheśvara,
how could these three names share the same essence as the ultimate tenet?
Therefore, it is said that one must not seek a distinct essence by relying on a common name.
Therefore, they employ characteristics to distinguish them.
Thus, they examine similarities to bring out differences and gather differences to achieve uniformity.
Whether differing or identical, they are all brought into a single ultimate.
Fifth, to apply one instance as an example for all:
this refers to the two paths of teaching and realization, as well as the dharmas possessed within a single mind;
it is not like the worldly attachment to a single momentary thought.
The Buddha-dharmadhātu is established as the object of contemplation;
while the former clarifies what is conceivable, the latter clarifies what is inconceivable, and so forth.
Within this section, there is only one passage that explains it.
By means of this single phrase, one harmonizes the upper and lower sections,
ensuring that the meaning of the text is thoroughly penetrating and clearly manifest throughout.
Sixth is the distinction between the universal and the specific regarding names and meanings.
Regarding the analogy of placing poison:
in the sutra, this serves only as an illustration that while the five destinies differ, the Buddha-nature remains unchanging;
the five flavors serve only as a metaphor for the varying intensity of the five periods within a single dispensation.
Though their intensity varies, all emerge from the ox;
now, following the principle of the text,
they pervade everywhere.
Whether determinate or indeterminate;
whether practice or person;
whether teaching or stage.
Sometimes, or in certain sections,
one cannot block the underlying meaning while merely clinging to the literal terminology;
thus, when poison is applied, there are two kinds of *amṛta* (clarified butter) that kill.
If one employs the five flavors, there are two kinds of milk that are unequal.
